paragraphs: “The court has resolved to go on with the trial. Meanwhile, I would like to make a few remarks on the portrait of Smerdyakov that the prosecutor drew with such subtlety and talent. I admire his talent, but I cannot agree with him. I have visited Smerdyakov. I have seen him and talked with him, and he made quite a different impression on me. His health was weak, it is true. But in character, in spirit, he was far from the weak man the prosecutor has made of him. I found no sign of the timidity the prosecutor made so much of. Nor was he simple. On the contrary, I found a deep distrust of everyone, hidden behind a mask of _naïveté_, and a mind of considerable reach. The prosecutor was too simple himself in taking him for feeble-minded. He made a very definite impression on me, and I came away convinced that he was a plainly spiteful creature, wildly ambitious, vengeful, and intensely envious. I made some inquiries. He resented his birth and was ashamed of it, and he would grind his teeth when he remembered that he was the son of ‘stinking Lizaveta.’ He was disrespectful to the servant Grigory and his wife, who had looked after him in his childhood. He cursed Russia and sneered at it. He dreamed of going to France and becoming a Frenchman. He often used to say that he had not the money for it. I believe he loved no one but himself, and he held a strangely high opinion of himself. His whole notion of culture came down to good clothes, clean shirt-fronts and polished boots. He believed himself to be Fyodor Pavlovitch’s illegitimate son (there is evidence of this), and he might well have resented his position beside his master’s legitimate sons. They had everything, and he had nothing. They had every right, they had the inheritance, while he was only the cook. He told me himself that he had helped Fyodor Pavlovitch put the notes into the envelope. The purpose of that sum—a sum that would have made his career—must have been hateful to him. Besides, he saw three thousand roubles in new rainbow-colored notes. (I asked him about that on purpose.) Oh, beware of showing an ambitious and envious man a great sum of money all at once! And it was the first time he had seen so much money in one man’s hands. The sight of those rainbow-colored notes may have left a morbid mark on his imagination, but with no immediate result.

“The talented prosecutor, with remarkable subtlety, set out for us all the arguments for and against the theory that Smerdyakov is guilty. In particular he asked what reason Smerdyakov could have had to fake a fit. But he may not have been faking at all. The fit may have come on quite naturally, and it may equally well have passed quite naturally. The sick man may have recovered—not fully, perhaps, but enough to regain consciousness, as happens with epileptics.

“The prosecutor asks at what moment Smerdyakov could have committed the murder. But it is very easy to name that moment. He might have woken out of a deep sleep (for he was only asleep—an epileptic fit is always followed by deep sleep) at the very moment when old Grigory shouted at the top of his voice, ‘Parricide!’ That shout in the dark and the silence may have woken Smerdyakov, whose sleep may by then have been lighter. He might quite naturally have been due to wake up an hour sooner.

“Getting out of bed, he goes almost without knowing it, with no clear purpose, toward the sound, to see what is wrong. His head is still muddled from his attack, and his mind is half asleep. But once he is in the garden he goes to the lighted windows, and his master, who would of course be glad to see him, gives him terrible news. His mind starts working at once. He hears every detail from his frightened master, and little by little, in his disordered brain, an idea takes shape—a terrible one, but tempting and irresistibly logical. Kill the old man, take the three thousand, and put all the blame on his young master. A terrible greed for money, for plunder, may have gripped him as he saw that he was safe from discovery. Oh, such sudden and irresistible impulses come so often when the chance is favorable, above all to murderers who never thought of committing murder beforehand. And Smerdyakov may have gone in and carried out his plan. With what weapon? Why, with any stone picked up in the garden. But why? For what purpose? Why, for the three thousand, which means a career for him. Oh, I do not contradict myself—the money may have existed. And perhaps Smerdyakov alone knew where to find it, where his master kept it. And the wrapping that held the money—the torn envelope on the floor?

“A little while ago the prosecutor was explaining his subtle theory that only an inexperienced thief like Karamazov would have left the envelope on the floor, and that a man like Smerdyakov would have taken care not to leave evidence against himself. As I listened, I felt I was hearing something very familiar. And, would you believe it, I had heard that very argument, that very guess at how Karamazov would have behaved, from Smerdyakov himself, exactly two days before. What is more, it struck me even then. I thought there was an artificial simplicity about him. I thought he was in a hurry to plant this idea in my mind, so that I would take it for my own. He slipped it in, so to speak. Did he not slip the same idea in at the inquiry, and suggest it to the talented prosecutor?

“I shall be asked, ‘What about the old woman, Grigory’s wife? She heard the sick man groaning close by, all night long.’ Yes, she heard it, but that testimony is highly unreliable. I once knew a lady who complained bitterly that a dog in the yard had kept her awake all night. Yet it turned out that the poor creature had yelped only once or twice. And that is natural. A man who is asleep hears a groan and wakes up, annoyed at being woken, but he drops off again at once. Two hours later he hears a groan again, wakes, and drops off again. Another two hours, and the same thing—three times in all during the night. In the morning the sleeper wakes and complains that someone was groaning all night and kept him awake. And it must seem that way to him. He has no memory of the two-hour stretches of sleep in between. He remembers only the moments of waking, so he feels he was awake all night.

“But why, why, asks the prosecutor, did Smerdyakov not confess in his last letter? Why did his conscience urge him to one step and not to the other? But forgive me: conscience implies repentance, and the suicide may have felt no repentance, only despair. Despair and repentance are two very different things. Despair may be vengeful and unforgiving, and a man who lays hands on himself may well have felt his hatred double for those he had envied all his life.

“Gentlemen of the jury, beware of a miscarriage of justice! What is there in all I have just laid before you that is so improbable? Find the flaw in my reasoning. Find the impossibility, the absurdity. And if there is only a shade of possibility, only a shade of probability in what I propose, do not condemn him. And is it only a shade? I swear by everything sacred that I fully believe in the account of the murder that I have just given. What troubles me and makes me indignant is this: of the whole mass of facts the prosecution has piled up against the prisoner, there is not one that is certain and beyond refutation. And yet the unhappy man is to be ruined by the sheer weight of these facts. Yes, the effect of the pile is awful: the blood, the blood dripping from his fingers, the bloodstained shirt, the dark night ringing with the shout ‘Parricide!’, and the old man falling with a broken head. And then the mass of phrases, statements, gestures, shouts! Oh, this has so much influence, it can so sway the mind. But, gentlemen of the jury, can it sway your minds? Remember that you have been given absolute power to bind and to loose. But the greater the power, the more terrible the responsibility.

“I do not withdraw one iota of what I have just said. But suppose, for a single moment, that I agreed with the prosecution that my luckless client did stain his hands with his father’s blood. This is only a supposition, I repeat. I never doubt his innocence for one instant. But so be it: I assume that my client is guilty of parricide. Even so, hear what I have to say. I have it in my heart to say something more to you, for I feel that a great struggle must be going on in your hearts and minds.... Forgive me for speaking of your hearts and minds, gentlemen of the jury, but I want to be truthful and sincere to the end. Let us all be sincere!”

At this point the speech was broken by rather loud applause. The last words had been spoken in such a sincere tone that everyone felt he really might have something to say, and that what he was about to say would matter very much. But the President heard the applause and announced in a loud voice that he would have the court cleared if it happened again. Every sound died away, and Fetyukovitch began in a voice full of feeling, quite unlike the tone he had used until then.
